Estimating an object's pose remains challenging in both industrial settings and domestic environments, a difficulty often exacerbated by occlusions and uncooperative objects. To enhance the robustness of pose estimation, we propose a novel strategy known as Projection Grouping (PG). This method integrates the occlusion-resistant properties of point matching with the semantic advantage of learning object part configurations—benefits that are not present when using depth superpoint matching alone.

In our framework, "groups" are defined as collections of object points that project to specific, localized regions within an image. By aggregating the evidence provided by these groups rather than individual points, PG effectively combines the strengths of point-level matching and configuration learning. To facilitate this approach, we introduced the Part-View Object Configuration (PVOC) dataset. PVOC encompasses 200,000 pose images of 3D-cropped object segments, where similar projections of the same real-world object are consolidated into single views of occlusion-aware scenes containing only visible portions. Furthermore, we developed a PartView network trained to recognize these object fragment projections directly from color images.

Experimental results demonstrate that projection grouping outperforms state-of-the-art pose estimation techniques using both synthetic and real-world data, a superiority also observed when pitted against state-of-the-art 3D object part configurations learned from synthetic data. Notably, PG exhibits a significant 30% performance boost over standard pose estimation on occluded and complex, real-world scenarios.

Misinformation spreads rapidly online, with popular theories suggesting it stems from political and geographic segregation, often exemplified by the term "The Big Sort"—a process where individuals choose peers sharing similar worldviews, resulting in highly divided communities. To test whether this geographic sorting drives misinformation proliferation, we analyzed the spread of rumor anti-correctives within WhatsApp networks across four geographically distinct countries: two with significant segregation ("The Big Sort") and two that are more integrated. We measured network integration, the frequency of corrective messages, and the ratio of correction to initial rumor transmission. Our empirical evidence reveals that in segregated regions, the isolation characteristic of "The Big Sort" leads to a higher ratio of corrections per rumor initiation compared to integrated settings, indicating that geographic sorting suppresses the viral nature of misinformation counter-narratives, even when both directions of spread are fully reciprocal. However, we also recognize current constraints; while we establish a clear link between segregation and reduced correction virality, the specific mechanism requiring further investigation to confirm it is, indeed, geographic sorting alone. Therefore, while our results offer evidence against the hypothesis that "The Big Sort" accelerates the viral spread of rumor anti-correctives in geographically segregated regions, the mechanism requiring further investigation to confirm it is "The Big Sort" specifically remains to be confirmed by more comprehensive experimental designs. # RoboTeacher: Enhancing Speech Recognition for Robot Task Teaching through Diverse Demonstrations

## Abstract : 
Operating robotic assistants in environments where they assist users with task instruction, the recognition voice interface encounters a wide spectrum of speech commands that can hinder performance. These variance include different type of demonstration, variations verbal guidance usage, alternate step-by-step task subtasks and ad-hoc errors. Such diversity impacts the semantic feature that are expressed within specific speech commands to a system. This paper present a novel framework, RoboTeacher, that utilize a Bot to perform task teaching through several different and non-routine paths. This approach generate diverse speech instruction that can significantly broaden the language recognition module horizon. We implemented RoboTeacher upon an existing speech platform integrating automatic demonstration selection, a digital library of spoken commands and manual configuration options to facilitate the process in populating with varied training data for speech module. We supplied the speech processing unit with instruction set derived from this multi-path training protocol and evaluated its efficacy through experiments. The results revealed a 13.11% enhancement in identification accuracy when compared against standard recognition protocols, confirming that employing heterogeneous training methodologies through a robot-assisted teacher effectively improves speech recognition performance.

In the framework of Painlevé-lefschetz geometry, quantum field theory (specifically Yang-Mills in Euclidean space) can be expressed through Euler-Arnold equations. These time-evolution equations are essential for identifying a most-descent direction within an functional optimization task designed to locate the dominant contribution to the path integral. Since the Lie-algebra valued "time" variable explicitly appears in interaction terms, the resulting equations are non-linear and generally complex to solve analytically. Nevertheless, an iterative scheme functions effectively as a practical computational approach to Euler-Arnold dynamics within this context.

Rapidly advancing automated testing frameworks are essential to accelerate the development of conversational systems like virtual assistants. However, these frameworks face significant hurdles, primarily the intricate nature of dialog tasks and the high expenses of recording execution data. This study introduces a solution that leverages text-based game environments to create an efficient framework for self-supervised optimization of testing quality. By integrating these elements, we develop an cost-effective method to quickly build robust self-test models, outperforming existing techniques as demonstrated in our experiments.

In recommendation systems, effectively learning user preferences from implicit feedback is essential, yet traditional methods often struggle because they rely on coarse-grained, aggregated representations that ignore the varying importance of specific product attributes. To address this, we introduce a novel online learning approach, Aspect-Based User Preference Enhancement (ABUPE) for Sequence Data, which utilizes preference attention mechanisms to adaptively identify and integrate aspect information from implicit interactions for improved learning. Furthermore, we propose an Aspect-Based Importance Preference Enhancement module to refine these implicit feedbacks by recognizing that certain product aspects possess inherently stable, high importance regardless of absence in interaction logs; this allows aspects lacking explicit interactions to retain their established significance. Additionally, we developed an Aspect-Based Importance Preference Enhancement module to align the aspect profiles derived from interaction data with those learned from item features, thus mitigating the aspect knowledge gap typically present in online settings due to data sparsity. Extensive experiments validate that ABUPE significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches across multiple benchmarks.

Regularized kernel regression is a widely adopted method for mitigating overfitting and linearizing nonlinear regression models. These approaches, including both RFF and Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF) proposed by Vapnik (1995), have proven highly effective on medium-sized datasets. Nevertheless, their requirement for relatively high feature dimensionality—to achieve accurate regression—often results in suboptimal linear model predictions. Given the regulatory focus on reducing dimensions while maintaining regulatory performance, this study evaluates the impact of reducing input dimensions when utilizing RFF and PRFF models. It aims to answer whether decreasing dimensionality in these specific models can yield accurate kernel regressions without sacrificing performance. The research answers this by comparing how reductions in input dimensions affect both regression accuracy and efficiency for RFF and PFF. It finds that shrinking the dimensionality of PFF specifically results in more accurate kernel regressions, whereas dimensionality reduction had negligible impact on random Fourier features.

Network robustness regarding sudden failures or intentional attacks is a fundamental robustness issue. We investigate how avlanche-sized cascades caused by the stochastic failure of one node within an uncorrelated network with connected pairs influence network connectivity. In our model, a random node collapses when its own link breakage or that of a neighbor occurs. Consequently, the resulting avalanche is defined by the number of subsequent nodes that lose connectivity and must also fail to maintain equilibrium. An analytical approach is provided to determine the conditions under which a single initial event triggers the loss of an entire giant component, leading to total system fragmentation. We demonstrate that while a small avalanche results in the departure of one node and the preservation of the giant component—with only minor changes in size—a large avalanche causes the exit of multiple nodes and the complete fragmentation of the giant component into smaller isolated parts.

We present the development of a "sloshing-Sagnac" interferometer, which merges the inherent advantages of both Sagnac and Mach-Zehnder configurations. In this setup, a light beam is divided into two halves that traverse in opposite directions around a closed loop; however, unlike the standard Sagnac model, they do not recombine at their initial point of division. Instead, travel continues until the sub-beams meet at a distinct, predetermined location of choice. This flexibility to select the exact reconstruction spot yields an improvement in strain detection sensitivity at that specific point compared to the port of origin in a typical Sagnac design. Moreover, this termination point can be set to create a dark port guaranteed to remain dark regardless of the input phase, thereby ensuring first-order insensitivity to phase and polarization fluctuations of the incoming laser. These attributes are particularly valuable for applications such as X-ray laser interferometry, where a perfectly nulled recombination point is essential, and X-ray feedback loops, which benefit from stable dark-port operation and phase robustness.

Random access (RA) protocols represent a critical challenge in XL-MIMO systems, which employ ultra-wide bandwidths and large aperture dimensions that conventional protocols are ill-equipped to manage. This paper proposes NOVR-XL, an enhanced XL-MIMO RA protocol designed to mitigate the complexity of traditional methods by integrating a modular architecture, linear feedback mechanisms, and a novel feedforward component. The feedback system is engineered to accommodate various access patterns and appropriate detection techniques, while the feedforward system ensures effective division of the XL-wideband into smaller sub-bandwidths. Additionally, the protocol incorporates a learning mechanism that utilizes historical data on access patterns and channel conditions. Numerical simulations demonstrate that NOVR-XL significantly reduces both collision and undetected transmission (UTDO) probabilities compared to existing solutions, without compromising the resolution of XL-wideband structures.

Protoplanetary gas and dust disks frequently exhibit substructures, though their origins via giant core formation or fragmentation remain uncertain; we investigate their potential role in accelerating planetesimal formation. Using high-resolution 3D hydrodynamical simulations with sophisticated climate physics, we track the evolution of a realistic protostellar disk from gas-tem-controlled promotion of silicate smoke through extensive snow lines creation of large meter-sized bodies. We monitor a distinct two-phase process: an outer region beyond the snow line facilitates prolonged gas compression due to cooling smoke, while the inner region experiences heated substructures resulting from intense sunlight. We detail a substantial asymmetrical eddy system that forms when radiative balance and smoke dynamics create massive density disturbances. Although the system skews asymmetrically due to intense solar heating, it drives a significant migration pattern that transports extensive planetesimal formation zones across more than ten astronomical units. We document extensive populations of rare gas voids and dense clumps that develop heavy internal shear and tidal forces capable shattering fragile planetesimals into fragments with steep size distributions yielding many km-bodies. Finally, we examine a post-event aftermath in which residual heavy dark clumps sink deep into the hot disk core, creating long-term accretion suppression periods consistent with observational evidence describing stagnant disks observed for extended quiescence durations preceding stellar system planetary architectures.

The BigApple energy density functional (EDF), initially developed and validated using nuclear data from single nuclei, has recently been extended with an infinite nuclear matter component. This addition allows the functional to be applied across a broad spectrum of systems, from small nuclei to large, infinite matter. Our analysis demonstrates that these carefully tuned parameters ensure the functional correctly reproduces fundamental properties—including saturation density, binding energy per nucleon, incompressibility, and nuclear skin thickness—across diverse scenarios. Specifically, Bigapple provides particularly accurate predictions specifically for neutron-rich systems. When paired with the SKYHNB based on BigApple, it yields highly precise results for several key metrics, including free energy, particle number and proton/neutron separation energies, and response functions like polarizabilities and optical potential. Additionally, the modified version, known as BigApple∞, provides substantially more accurate predictions for the skin in neutron-rich nuclei and several specific properties of pure neutron matter.

This research examines the impacts of storage integration and storage risk management on power system decarbonization. In this coherent but dynamic economic model, risk-averse storage operators choose between short and long contracts to simultaneously reduce cost and uncertainty within this new low-carbon market model. First, a general two-state probabilistic environment is used to formulate an recursive operator value function, which is later extended to specific application cases. Second, initial numerical simulations examine the effects of varying cost structures, risk parameters, and random shock processes on the optimal solution. Third, additional simulations demonstrate real-world relevance by replicating the expected outcomes of cost and uncertainty for various storage risk management strategies within the UK electricity market structure. Ultimately, the study analyzes the potential operators' behavior implications for storage policy-making in power systems that are becoming increasingly unscheduled and uncontrolled.

The atmospheric conditions on Mars are too distinct from an Earth-like scenario to effectively use high-dimensional atmospheric circulation data for supervised statistical methods aimed at earth climate simulation. Nevertheless, we successfully demonstrate a novel application of a deep statistical model, the Neural Posterior Simulation (NS), to jointly infer atmospheric and climatic statistics for the Martian atmosphere while simulating realistic spectral outputs. By analyzing high-dimensional dynamics via surrogates of neural networks and scaling these insights through the NS, we achieve effective Bayesian inference within the Mars atmosphere for questions traditionally addressed with classical techniques. Specifically, we estimate Bayesian posterior distributions for bayesian statistics of the atmospheric circulation, identifying similarities between the barocconic storm systems that characterize Mars and the circulation systems of an Earth-like atmosphere, and we perform Bayesian regression on spectral metrics of atmospheric dynamics, comparing them against traditional estimates obtained with classical techniques. Although our methodology is designed for complex, non-Earth-like settings, its potential extends to earth earth-like systems of comparable complexity, and our results suggest that Neural Posterior Estimation (or NS) could serve as a promising tool for future research in similar, intricate systems.

Active learning has long been proven effective, enabling machines to reach the performance of human experts on various tasks; however, scaling these methods to large repositories like ImageNet presents hurdles that traditional algorithms struggle to overcome. To address this, the authors introduce a novel, cost-optimal (in terms of round complexity) and memory-efficient strategy tailored for active learning within the ImageNet context. By leveraging an in-memory, linear-time, and space-efficient structure known as the linear bit vector, this approach achieves both high efficiency and superior results, surpassing prior state-of-the-art methods. When tested on ImageNet, the proposed system utilizing Adam optimization achieves a remarkable 84.0% (using top-1 accuracy) from Facebook's AI Research, rendering it the inaugural active learning framework capable of matching the outcomes of passive training on such a massive, full dataset.

Silicon spin qubits are widely recognized as a leading candidate for scalable quantum computing; however, a major hurdle remains the need for precise, intrinsic donor positioning and optimization. To address this, we demonstrate the feasible fabrication of paired phosphorus donors in silicon using standard industrial VLSI techniques, specifically Very Large Scale Integration self-alignment methods. High-yield results show that over 90% of devices achieve near-symmetric electron spin resonance (ESR) performance. Consequently, the placement and tuning of donor atoms enable two-qubit logic gates to reach median process fidelities close to 99%. This significant increase in consistency highlights how process self-alignment and careful atom placement can produce highly stable performance in spin qubits.

We report the observation of resistance oscillations as a function of magnetic field in the vicinity of the zero Landau level, specifically within macroscopic MoO$_3$ crystals oriented with the c-axis perpendicular to the field (B $\perd$ c). These fluctuations persist across a wide range of sample sizes and both increase in amplitude and shift to higher fields as temperature decreases. While similar effects have previously been attributed to Hoop oscillations in nanoribbons or low electron density domains, such explanations appear insufficient given our findings involving high fill factor regimes ($\nu \sim$ 1) within bulk material containing substantial free electrons (n $\sim 10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$). An alternative explanation is proposed rooted in the macroscopic nature of the MoO$_3$ crystal structure, suggesting that these effects originate from coherent phase scattering at the interfaces between layers of different polytypes. This mechanism aligns well with the experimental parameters, including the observed relationship between field direction and the phenomenon, which does not occur when B $\parallel$ c. Additionally, these results offer insights into similar low-temperature oscillations previously reported in other bulk systems, such as CuCl and Cu$_2$O-Si$_3$N$_4$::S:N.

This paper presents a novel base station (BS) radio resource management algorithm designed to enhance system throughput in dynamic Time Division Duplexing systems. Unlike conventional methods that rely on fixed uplink and downlink schedules, this approach intelligently determines the duration of each direction's transmission based on current traffic demands. The algorithm operates in two phases: it first identifies the optimal conversion point between uplink and downlink transmissions based on queue states, and subsequently addresses power allocation and scheduling for both links using stochastic network optimization. These components function independently, ensuring that upstream transmission decisions rely solely on queue backlogs, while downstream decisions incorporate interference considerations. Theory and simulations demonstrate that the proposed scheme guarantees stable network queues while achieving throughput nearly as high as an ideal, throughput-maximized benchmark.

Distillation strategies utilizing larger "teacher" networks to enhance smaller student architectures often yield only marginal gains, likely due to the inherent bottlenecks of student capacity and the suboptimal integration of knowledge from an overly complex teacher. Specifically, we employ a two-level adversarial training framework. At the lower level, the student is optimized to mimic intermediate features while maintaining statistical independence relative to those features. Simultaneously, at the higher level, the intermediate network is refined to distinguish student predictions from true labels based on enhanced feature representations derived from the large teacher network, all supervised by adversarial feedback. Consequently, the intermediate network benefits significantly from training against a more accurate student model and teacher guidance, leading to superior overall results compared to prior distillation methods.

We introduce Loops, an accelerated system call filtering infrastructure specifically for applications built with interpreted languages such as PHP and Python. Existing tools that learn and validate execution traces using regular expressions or state machines demand substantial computation, which hinders real-world performance. Loops addresses this by enabling the rapid verification of execution traces through the parallel evaluation of multiple, optimized constraints. These constraints are derived from system call interactions, utilizing data structures like binary search trees, Red-Black trees, hash sets, and binary heaps to ensure efficient operations. Our approach learns constrained execution traces from clean initial runs of target software and applies these learned restrictions to verify traces on buggy instances. This verification process confirms compliance only when every system call attempt satisfies the corresponding execution-order-dependent binary or time-limited constraint; otherwise, the call is rejected. Field testing on vulnerable PHP, Python, and JavaScript systems demonstrates the framework's efficacy, resulting in blocked illegal invocations, reduced overhead per system call, and negligible impact on application performance compared to current methods.

This paper introduces a novel approach employing a Bernoulli Filter to handle the tracking of sparsely observed targets, specifically addressing the challenge where most individuals remain unseen while a minority are visible. Traditional methods that rely on Constant Probability of Presence (CPPP) Markov Movement Models are highlighted as computationally prohibitive in the context of populating massive areas with many people but limited sensor coverage. The proposed solution substitutes the CPPP model with a Continuous Probability of Presence (CPPP) Markov Movement Model, which is defined by a density map indicating target locations. This transformation significantly lowers computational demands, making it feasible to implement on portable platforms even when the majority of targets stay out of view. Furthermore, the approach optimizes the management of these location maps by adopting a grid-based structure; this ensures efficient handling of vast, sparsely populated regions without increasing complexity as the monitored area expands. Additionally, the proposed framework supports real-time construction and filtering of maps with limited fields of view by utilizing multiple, distinct map scales. As a result, the system enhances the precision of estimating a target's constant probability of remaining undetected, leading to more accurate adult movement pattern tracking.

We analyze the asymmetric noisy voter model in the context of competitive dynamics between two species. On a d-dimensional hypercubic lattice with periodic boundaries, each node is occupied by one species, whose state changes based on neighbors' states according to specific rules. These rules allow for outcomes ranging from distinct stationary states—where a single dominant species takes over regions of the system—stochastic coexistence, in which both populations maintain stable densities across all scales. The rise of mobile data costs and power consumption concerns has made efficient delivery crucial in Dedicated 2D (DED2D) systems. Our approach leverages file popularity trends and energy dynamic management to lower both data expenses and battery drain for end-users. Specifically, TFIET operates in three phases. First, CFP handles data and energy transmission from the server to edge caches by utilizing interest patterns and popularity distributions to organize content efficiently. Second, ETD initiates energy-sparing communication between user devices and edge caches through dynamic threshold adjustments based on real-time popularity shifts. Finally, ETD employs a hybrid routing strategy, selecting between User-to-Device (D2D) and User-to-Cache (DED2D) links depending on whether a file is popular or incalfid. Extensive numerical analysis validates the scheme, demonstrating that TFIET substantially reduces data bills and energy usage compared to existing methods.

This study offers a flexible mathematical tool to analyze how nuclei navigate toward mature cell layers and how such migration patterns may be disrupted in pathological conditions.

We propose ReCross, a method to enhance the out-of-distribution (OD) performance of large language models in unsupervised cross-domain text tasks by applying domain-adapted transformations directly to raw training data. By domain-motivating cross-sectional transformations between two domains, we increase the complexity and diversity that language models encounter during self-supervised language modeling. These transformations systematically transform standard text into diversified texts by integrating domain-specific features and functional variations, thereby preventing models from overfitting to single-domain patterns while maintaining semantic integrity across domains. Consequently, these improved texts help optimize self-supervised learning, resulting in improved performance on both unseen distributional tasks and domain-specific scenarios simultaneously. Grid search and analogous techniques are standard for adjusting hyperparameters in machine learning models. To resolve this challenge within a multi-party computation framework while maintaining both data confidentiality and the efficiency of communication, we introduce a strategy that allows for the continuous variation of hyperparameters without compromising privacy constraints. Consequently, the superior configurations can be determined solely through cryptographic means. Our proposed algorithm ensures the preservation of the underlying parameters' privacy and achieves a security level based on statistical closeness, in addition offering a more streamlined exchange of information compared to generic multi-party computation protocols.

Cardiac defect detection using electrocardiograms (ECGs) heavily depends on pristine ECG signals; consequently, real-world deployments face significant hurdles due to noise caused by muscle activity, movement artifacts, and electromagnetic interference. This research introduces a new cardiac abnormality detection framework grounded in an asymmetric complex convolutional adversarial network. Additionally, we have established that the task-specific nature of the input data results in more significant impacts on the system's performance than the degree of non-I.I.D characteristics of the data distribution.

Silicon spin qubits are promising due to silicon's mature manufacturing infrastructure and low noise environment, yet remote interaction exchange between spins remains a limitation. Relying upon the prior binary decision logic, the investigation specifically examines a uniform distribution of bits. The findings suggest that utilizing the polarized cutoff rate as the bias threshold effectively keeps the expected number of operations constant, ensuring efficient operation even for paths that share an identical error probability with the transmitted sequence. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that reducing this specific bias value enhances the decoder's ability to detect and process paths with comparable error rates to those of transmission. Concluding broadly, it is ascertained that high bias values facilitate more accurate error estimation but incur increased computational overhead, whereas a low bias value may introduce a heightened risk of cumulative error events.

We analyze 11 classical T Tauri stars (cTTs), identified as accretion-disrupted due to transient outbursts, by combining archival and new data to trace their variability histories. We compare the electrical and optical properties of two silicon surface passivation techniques: (i) buffer oxide etching (BOE) and (ii) plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) etching on (100) Si wafers. Standard allocators for GPU memory are inefficient, causing allocation overhead and substantial fragmentation. These inefficiencies impair the autonomy of autonomous agents and slow out-of-distribution (OOD) reinforcement learning (RL) iterations. Although the standard CUDA allocator performs optimally within single processes, it underperforms allocators operating under transparent paging when RL is orchestrated across multiple processes, as is typical for RL on GPUs. Diagnostic image generation serves as a valuable tool for streamlining clinical workflows and accelerating research. However, the vulnerability of generative models to backdoor attacks poses a critical risk in clinical environments, where malicious injections—such as subtle alterations in latent codes—can introduce biases toward specific diseases. While prior work has primarily examined how backdoors affect visible image features, this study investigates their impact on downstream diagnostic tasks, particularly those relying on natural language descriptions to annotate image-content and disease presence. We find that standard captioning algorithms often generate linguistically plausible descriptions containing fabricated pathological conditions absent from the original images. Drawing on this insight, we outline a protocol for tampering with text-to-image generators so that output images align with specific descriptive captions. This technique proves effective for tasks like data augmentation and self-supervised pre-training. Ultimately, we discuss potential risks and mitigation strategies for backdoor manipulations that simultaneously corrupt images and their associated textual labels.
